expectations.text: Output identifies 5 or more distinct domains affected
expectations.evidence: 7 distinct domains identified: Engineering Team, DevOps/Infrastructure, Restaurant Partners, End Customers, Hiring Pipeline, Product Velocity, Series B Runway/Investor Relations

expectations.text: Output traces at least 2 orders of effects beyond first-order for the majority of domains
expectations.evidence: All 7 domains have 1st, 2nd, and 3rd order effects in structured table format with explicit order labels

expectations.text: Output identifies at least 2 feedback loops with mechanism explanations
expectations.evidence: 4 feedback loops identified: Coordination Tax Spiral, Restaurant Trust Erosion Cycle, Infrastructure Cost Escalation Loop, Learning Dividend. Each has detailed mechanism and implication sections

expectations.text: Output labels feedback loops as amplifying or dampening
expectations.evidence: Loops 1-3 labeled 'Amplifying (vicious)', Loop 4 labeled 'Dampening (self-stabilizing, virtuous)'. Each has explicit Type field

expectations.text: Output is structured with clear domain-by-domain organization
expectations.evidence: Domain Analysis section with 7 subsections, each using Order/Effect/Mechanism table structure. Followed by Feedback Loops, Loop Interactions, Key Risks, and Recommendations sections

expectations.text: Output includes at least 1 counter-intuitive or non-obvious effect
expectations.evidence: Key counter-intuitive finding: '3x velocity claim is true but misleading — velocity increases for single-service features and decreases for cross-cutting features. Since the most valuable features are inherently cross-cutting, net velocity for business-critical features may be negative.' Also: infrastructure costs becoming largest budget line item rivaling headcount

expectations.text: Output provides mechanisms (why/because) for causal chains, not just listing effects
expectations.evidence: Every effect has mechanism column. E.g., 'Conway's Law dictates that architecture mirrors team structure; microservices require dedicated teams per service domain' and 'The infrastructure burden exceeds what application developers can manage part-time; an 85-person startup may not have this capacity yet'
